sentence: Exploring Semantic Perturbations on Grover CMSC 473/673: Capstone in Machine Learning Ziqing Ji, Pranav Kulkarni, Marko Neskovic, Kevin Nolan, Yan Xu 21 December 2021 https://github.com/itspranavk/cmsc473fall21-grover Abstract With news and information being as easy to access as they currently are, it is more important than ever to ensure that people are not mislead by what they read.
label: none

sentence: Recently, the rise of neural fake news (AI-generated fake news) and its demonstrated effectiveness at fooling humans has prompted the development of models to detect it.
label: none

sentence: One such model is the Grover model, which can both detect neural fake news to prevent it, and generate it to arXiv:2302.00509v2 [cs.LG] 25 Jul 2024 demonstrate how a model could be misused to fool human readers.
label: none

sentence: In this work we explore the Grover model’s fake news detection capabilities by performing targeted attacks through perturbations on input news articles.
label: none

sentence: Through this we test Grover’s resilience to these adversarial attacks and expose some potential vulnerabilities which should be addressed in further iterations to ensure it can detect all types of fake news accurately. 1 Introduction and Literature 1.1 The Rise of Machine-Generated Fake News While the term “fake news” has become politically charged in recent years, researchers of online misinformation typically define it as a form of propaganda that knowingly transmits false information to readers, viewers, or users [2].
label: none

sentence: This definition is rather broad, with many academics offering their own take.
label: none

sentence: Alcott and Gentzkow describe fake news as “news articles that are intentionally and verifiably false, and could mislead readers” [1].
label: none

sentence: Wardle and Derakhshan posit seven categories of fake news, which together make a scale ranging from simple satire to fully fabricated content [13].
label: none

sentence: For the purposes of this project, we will define fake news as any text that is created with the intention of imparting false information onto the reader to achieve the goal of the disseminator.
label: none

sentence: This includes, as Zellers et Al. describe, “targeted propaganda that closely mimics the style of real news” [16].
label: none

sentence: Taken this way, fake news has been present in social and political discourse for thousands of years.
label: none

sentence: In one of the earliest cited examples of fake news, Ramses the Great of Ancient Egypt spread propaganda portraying the Battle of Kadesh as a glowing victory for Egypt over the Hittites.
label: none

sentence: The Treaty of Kadesh reveals that in fact, the battle ended in stalemate [14].
label: none

sentence: In the modern era, fake news can pose great threats in democracy, politics, economy, and so on [5, 1, 12].
label: none

sentence: Creating and consuming high quality misinformation is notably easier over the internet compared to print media [11, 1].
label: none

sentence: The current deep learning methods in natural language processing [4, 9] can automatically generate texts, and they can be applied to fake news generation, making it harder to tell whether a given article is authentic or fake.
label: none

sentence: This change in ease has caused a dramatic increase in the proliferation of fabricated content using social media [8]. 1.2 An Algorithmic Response Lazer et al. asserted in 2018 that the rise of fake news prompts “a new system of safeguards” [8].
label: none

sentence: Social media companies have since adopted several strategies to detect and remove fake news from their websites.
label: none

sentence: For obvious reasons, none of these strategies have been made publicly available.
label: none

sentence: However, a good body of research on fake news detection is accessible to the wider public.
label: none

sentence: Shu et Al. describe fake news detection from a data mining perspective.
label: none

sentence: They focus more on social engagement, click-through rate, and share counts rather than the actual content of social media posts to determine what is legitimate [11].
label: none

sentence: Reis et Al. created a new system of features and measures for use in supervised learning pertaining to fake news detection [10].
label: none

sentence: Zhou et al. lay out a multidisciplinary approach in which they “broadly adopt techniques in data mining, machine learning, natural language processing, information retrieval, and social search” [17].
label: none

sentence: It is clear that there are a plethora of existing techniques to detect and address fake news in social media, but it is uncertain how well these techniques perform on real-world data.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, it is unclear what vulnerabilities they possess.
label: none

sentence: Our proposed paper will examine types of vulnerabilities in Grover, a state-of-the-art framework for detecting fake news. 1 1.3 GPT-2 and Grover In early 2019, AI research company Open AI released GPT-2, a “large transformer-based language model with 1.5 billion parameters” [9].
label: none

sentence: GPT-2 is remarkably good at synthesising new text given a prefix.
label: none

sentence: While it still under- performs human ability, the model has broken algorithmic records in accuracy and perplexity on several datasets.
label: none

sentence: The incredible accuracy of GPT-2 has led to some concern over its ethical use.
label: none

sentence: Floridi and Chiriatti argue that with such technology, “Readers and consumers of texts will have to get used to not knowing whether the source is artificial or human” [18].
label: none

sentence: Zeller et Al, however, focus on GPT’s implications on fake news [16].
label: none

sentence: They conclude that GPT-2 and related technologies pose a significant threat to the validity of online information.
label: none

sentence: The assumption is that GPT is highly capable of creating texts that fool both humans and machines, allowing for an even greater proliferation of fake news on the internet.
label: none

sentence: To counter this threat, Zeller and his team created a state-of-the-art tool named Grover.
label: none

sentence: Grover is both a neural fake news generator and detector.
label: none

sentence: It is built using the same architecture as GPT2 [9].
label: none

sentence: It considers five metadata fields of an article: domain, date, authors, headline, and body.
label: none

sentence: The design of the model allows for flexible decomposition of the joint distribution.
label: none

sentence: During inference, the model uses the fields as context where each field contains its content and field-specific tokens.
label: none

sentence: The tokens are concatenated and appended with the target field-specific token to generate the target field.
label: none

sentence: During training, they separate metadata fields into two sets F1 and F2, where they minimize the cross entropy loss of predicting tokens in F1 followed by F2.
label: none

sentence: As is shown in the experiments, Grover noticeably improves on perplexity when conditioned on metadata, and it is over 5 perplexity points lower than GPT2 models.
label: none

sentence: Humans are Easily Fooled by Grover-written propaganda.
label: none

sentence: Also, Grover performs best at detecting Grover’s fake news compared with GPT2, BERT, and FastText [7].
label: none

sentence: Simple techniques aren’t enough to consistently fool Grover.
label: none

sentence: For example, rejection sampling produces only a temporary advantage to a hypothetical attacker, because once Grover is trained on additional generations from that attacker, its accuracy returns to levels we expect [15]. 1.4 Vulnerabilities in Fake News Detection Currently, there is no substantial research on the robustness of fake news detectors.
label: none

sentence: To fill this gap, we would like to research the vulnerabilities of Grover, as it is the best-performing detector to date.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, we will design attacks at the word, sentence, paragraph, and article (i.e discourse) level to analyze Grover’s performance in detecting fake news.
label: none

sentence: Some attacks include replacing single words with synonyms, rearranging phrases within sentences, and breaking up the “narrative structure” of an article.
label: none

sentence: We hope to determine how much and what parts of a text need to be changed before Grover will miscategorize it.
label: none

sentence: In conducting this research, we will provide analysis that can be used to make Grover and similar systems more robust, with the ultimate goal of improving validity in online texts. 2 Getting Started 2.1 Setting up Grover As part of Zeller’s goal of ensuring transparency in neural fake news detectors and generators, the Grover source code is publicly available on GitHub here: https://github.com/rowanz/grover However, setting up Grover was one of the hardest parts of this project.
label: none

sentence: The version of Grover available on GitHub has numerous inconsistencies and bugs that make it hard to set up and generate useful results.
label: none

sentence: Some of these issues include: • Inconsistencies between naming conventions.
label: none

sentence: For example, large and medium models, article and text fields, etc. • Given discriminator does not consider article content to classify. • Multiple authors are not supported.
label: none

sentence: Authors must be converted from list to string. • Setting up models for generation and discrimination was poorly documented.
label: none

sentence: As part of our research project, we will include a fixed version of the run discrimination.py file in our GitHub repository that address some of the above concerns, in addition to providing an in-depth explanation of how to set up Grover for discrimination. 2.2 Selection of Grover Model There are three main types of models offered by Zeller’s team: Base, Large/Medium, and Mega.
label: none

sentence: Each model can do generation and discrimination (using checkpoints).
label: none

sentence: For our purpose, we decided to use the Large model because it provided a balance between accuracy and computational requirements.
label: none

sentence: More specifically, we used the 2 model generator=medium ∼ discriminator=grover ∼ discsize=medium ∼ dataset=p=0.96 located in Zeller’s Google cloud bucket.
label: none

sentence: This enabled us not only to get valid results with top − p = 0 . 96, but also enabled us to run the model locally on our computers.
label: none

sentence: Eventually, for larger scale tests, we used Google cloud TPUs to speed up the process. 2.3 Analysis of Large Grover Model • Vocabulary size: 50720 • Hidden Layers: 24 • Neurons per hidden layer: 1024 • Activation: GELU 3 Uninformed Perturbations The goal of making uninformed perturbations is to explore Grover’s sensitivity to changes on word, sentence, and discourse-level.

label: none

sentence: We, as humans, are incredible good at detecting nonsensical article flow, but we want to explore Grover’s sensitivity to such changes.

sentence: Subjective sentences generally refer to personal opinions, emotions or judgements, whereas more objective sentences refer to facts. and we wanted to test whether inserting sentences of different subjectivity values have an effect on Grover’s performance.
label: none

label: none

sentence: Out of the 8 articles from the mini testing dataset, 5 of them show that the generated machine-written article tend to be more subjective than the original human-written ones, as shown in 7 Figure 7: Overall Subjectivity We generated the dataset for testing the effect of subjectivity through inserting sentences from the machine- written article (the fake sentences) into the human-written one.
label: none

sentence: However, we insert them following a certain order.
label: none

label: none

sentence: Therefore, since the machine-generated articles tend to be more subjective, we would expect that if we insert the most subjective sentences first, the confidence level of the ”human” class would start to drop sooner, compared to the articles where the least subjective sentences are inserted first.

sentence: However, after some more insertions, Grover becomes less sure and we see the model jumping between human and machine-written classification. 3.2 Word-Level Substitutions In order to assess the performance of Grover at the word level, we tested the effect of swapping words with their synonyms within articles.
label: none

sentence: For each article (having length n words), a word was chosen at random and was replaced with a synonym using the NLTK wordnet.
label: none

sentence: The new article was then saved in a JSON file and the process was repeated again.
label: none

sentence: This procedure produced a set of n articles, where the first article had one synonym swapped, the second article had two synonyms, and so on.
label: none

sentence: The set was run through the Grover discriminator to test the model’s performance on each article.
label: none

sentence: (a) Human-Written Article (b) Machine-Written Article Figure 9: Synonym Substitution As seen in Figure 9a and Figure 9b, swapping synonyms in this way had no effect on Grover’s ability to classify articles.
label: none

sentence: This finding was expected for the case of machine-written articles, as swapping synonyms does nothing to make an underlying article more ”human.” However, in the human-written case, the result was surprising.
label: none

sentence: Similar to the sentence swap experiment in section 3.1, we expected Grover’s classification to shift toward ’Machine’ as more synonyms were substituted in an article.
label: none

sentence: The fact that the classification remained the same is likely due to two factors.
label: none

sentence: First, only some of the words in each article had true synonyms.
label: none

sentence: Proper nouns, for example, were unable to be substituted.
label: none

sentence: Likewise, certain parts 9 of speech had no synonyms.
label: none

sentence: Articles such as a and the , and conjunctions like but or and are examples of such words.
label: none

sentence: On average, we were only able to generate synonyms for fifty to sixty percent of the words in a given article.
label: none

sentence: It is possible that swapping a higher number of words would lead to the expected effect.
label: none

sentence: The second factor is related to how Grover perceives an article’s ”flow” when classifying.
label: none

sentence: As discussed in sections 3.1 and 3.1.3, Grover is heavily influenced by changes at the discourse level.
label: none

sentence: It could be that swapping synonyms in the above way doesn’t impact the underlying structure of an article enough for Grover to perceive the changes as meaningful.
label: none

sentence: While these two factors are likely, More research is needed in order to determine exactly why Grover behaves in this way. 3.3 GPT-2 Substitutions The original Grover paper particularly emphasized the dangers of pre-existing language models like GPT-2 and BERT, which can also be used to generate fake news.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, they noted that Grover performed extremely well on GPT-2 generated articles even though it had never seen GPT-2 generated articles during training, achieving 96.1% accuracy [15].
label: none

sentence: Given that Grover was not trained on GPT-2, and the testing done in the original experiment was on a relatively small set of data (500 generations), we felt that exploring perturbations using GPT-2 generations could yield promising results. 3.3.1 Setup Perturbations using GPT-2 were all done using Deep AI’s Text Generation API [3].
label: none

sentence: The generator is not the original GPT-2 model but rather a modified version of the original, and provides capabilities for word, sentence, and paragraph completion.
label: none

sentence: For the purposes of our experiment, we refer to generations using this modified model as still being GPT-2 generations.
label: none

sentence: We chose to explore sentence and paragraph completion, since they provide more context than single word generation and are more representative of an attack someone would want to perform to fool a reader.
label: none

sentence: For the experiment we used 8 original human-written articles, and replaced portions of the articles using GPT-2 generations, gradually increasing the percentage of the article that is GPT2-generated.
label: none

sentence: First, the original article is loaded in and a sentence or paragraph is extracted.
label: none

sentence: That text is then fed into the API and a GPT2-generated text is returned (usually multiple sentences or paragraphs).
label: none

sentence: Next, the first sentence or paragraph is extracted from the generated text, and quotations/apostrophes replaced so it can be properly tokenized.
label: none

sentence: Finally, the first sentence or paragraph occurring after the original piece of text is replaced with the generation, since the model works in a predictive fashion. 3.3.2 Results Overall, substituting GPT-2 generations into real articles showed varying but generally promising results.
label: none

sentence: For both sentence and paragraph replacement, certain articles were classified as machine-generated very early, but most were not classified as such until a significant portion of the article was replaced.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, while there did exist slight variations between sentence and paragraph replacement, the two produced very similar results and classification patterns, which reinforces both that the GPT-2 generator is good at both sentence and paragraph generation, and that similar context for the language model is provided by both sentences and paragraphs, and both are greater than that of word substitution.
label: none

sentence: In Figures 10a and 10b we see that both paragraph and sentence replacement for article 1 were detected immediately, representing good detection by Grover.
label: none

sentence: Conversely, Figures 10c and 10d show that a significant portion of article 6 had to be replaced before Grover consistently classified it as machine-written.
label: none

sentence: All four figures demonstrate the similar classification patterns that were often seen between the two substitution types.
label: none

sentence: We also observed an interesting phenomenon can be seen when replacing the sentences of article 2 and 3, as depicted in Figure 11.
label: none

sentence: At moments during the replacement, it seems as if Grover has ”caught on” (classified as machine-written with high probability) that the article is partially machine written.
label: none

sentence: Then, an effectively generated GPT-2 sentence causes the model to go back to classifying incorrectly, as is the case with the 6th and 21st substituted sentences for articles 2 and 3, respectively.
label: none

sentence: This demonstrates that GPT-2 substitutions can have vastly different (and sometimes surprisingly effective) effects on Grover’s ability to classify.
label: none

sentence: This is likely because each substitution generation is based on a certain context; if Grover was trained on certain contexts and sequences of words, then it will perform better on them versus those that it hasn’t seen before.
label: none

sentence: This again reiterates the benefit of GPT2-based attacks, since Grover has little prior experience with them.
label: none

sentence: Ultimately though, our experiments show that despite certain variations, Grover is generally performs badly up to a certain portion of substitutions.
label: none

sentence: To measure this, we define a value–undetected substitution percentage–which is the percentage of paragraphs or sentences substituted before Grover was able to consistently classify the modified article as machine-generated.
label: none

sentence: As shown in Table 1, the mean undetected substitution percentage was 24.4% for paragraph substitution and 23.1% for sentence substitution, with individual article values ranging from less than 10% to over 35% for both types.
label: none

sentence: While our experiments were conducted on a small set of articles, these results indicate that attacks on small portions of the article are unlikely to be detected by Grover’s classifier.
label: none

sentence: Similar to generating adversarial examples for images, we could apply the Fast Gradient Signed Method [6] to generate the adversarial embedding table.
label: none

sentence: We first input the sentences to be perturbed into the classifier and get the loss.
label: none

sentence: We now have the gradient of loss w.r.t. the embedding table.
label: none

sentence: Then we choose different steps ( ϵ = 0 . 001 , 0 . 1 , 1 , 5) times the gradient and add that to the embedding table.
label: none

sentence: For all the tokens in the input sentences, there is gradient information for all those tokens.
label: none

sentence: We then try to find a different token whose original embedding is similar to the adversarial embedding of the token.
label: none

sentence: We choose the cosine similarity of the normalized embeddings and during the experiments, we found that a threshold of 0.18 is great to find similar embeddings while only changing one or two words in the original article.
label: none

sentence: After we find the token pair to replace, we encode the original article to get the tokens, use the corresponding token to replace the attacked token, and decode it to a new article.
label: none

sentence: One benefit is that since we are changing the same tokens, the probability distribution is unchanged.
label: none

sentence: Therefore, the perplexity remains the same after perturbations.
label: none

sentence: The token pair finding algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1.
label: none

sentence: Query-Dependent Zero-Shot Prompting for Arithmetic Reasoning: Opportunities and Chal- lenges.

sentence: Out of the many attempts, prompting — a natural language prefix or instruction that ex- plains how to complete the task — stands out as a lightweight promising solution for eliciting the capabilities of LLMs without model parameter tuning (Wei et al., 2022).

sentence: While the advances in zero-shot prompting strategies (Kojima et al., 2022) highlight the potential in finding effective query-independent solutions, its reliance on manual crafting efforts and the vast search space over natural language intensifies the difficulty in discovering effective prompts (Deng et al., 2022).

sentence: This study aims to augment the arithmetic reasoning capacities of LLMs, a capability considered cru- cial (OpenCompass, 2023; Liu et al., 2023a).

sentence: Challenge 1: Inference Time Evaluation is Hard.
label: none

sentence: A primary challenge arises in evaluating the effectiveness of prompts during inference, especially when the true answer to a query is not known a priori.
label: none

sentence: For arithmetic reasoning, enumerating many potentially effective prompts and enquire language models with those prompted queries will only result in a batch of answers, yet determining which response is correct in the absence of a ground-truth label requires extra non-trivial effort.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, the computational cost associated with this prompt enumeration process is substantial.
label: none

sentence: Challenge 2: Online Prompt Evaluation and Optimization is Expensive.
label: none

sentence: On the other hand, searching for potentially effective prompts heavily relies on expensive online evaluation.
label: none

sentence: In the lit- erature, evaluating the effectiveness of a proposed prompt requires assessing its performance on multiple datasets and LLMs, to show its distributional superiority over the others.
label: none

sentence: In the arith- metic reasoning task, using the GPT-3.5-turbo API (OpenAI, 2023) to evaluate a single prompt on a medium-sized dataset with 10k query-answer pairs will lead to an ≈ $1 cost, yet learning from trials and errors often requires millions of interactions even for tasks with a few actions to choose from (Schulman et al., 2017).
label: none

sentence: The vast action space of natural language further increases the pro- hibitive cost for such interactive search (Zhang et al., 2022a; Deng et al., 2022).

sentence: A E D P -OIRL RLHF XTENDED ISCUSSION ON ROMPT AND A.1 C ONNECTIONS AND D IFFERENCE FROM A D ESCRIPTIVE P ERSPECTIVE To better understand our contribution, it would be helpful to link and contrast Prompt-OIRL with the framework of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or AI feedback (RLAIF).
label: none

sentence: In general, the success of RLHF and RLAIF motivates our idea of integrating human expertise in prompting, and Prompt-OIRL can be interpreted as a special type of prompt policy learning from offline AI feedback, which differentiates from existing literature.
label: none

sentence: The fact that Prompt-OIRL first learns a reward model and then performs policy optimization using the reward model makes the method related to RLHF and RLAIF.
label: none

sentence: From such a perspective, Prompt- OIRL treats prompt evaluation and optimization as a process of aligning prompting strategies with the preferences of the LLMs , contrasting to aligning LLM responses with human preferences.
label: none

sentence: In analogy with the RLHF that improves the performance of LLMs with regard to human preferences, we hypothesize that such a perspective could lead to more effective prompts while avoiding the need for random exploration of the prompt space, which is computationally expensive.
label: none

sentence: That said, there are several key differences that make Prompt-OIRL distinguishable from the existing RLHF and RLAIF literature.
label: none

sentence: RLHF (or RLAIF) often includes the following steps: 1. sampling from pre-trained language models to generate dialogue data; 2. human (or AI) raters are then asked to rank those generated data according to given criteria such as harmless and helpful; 3. a preference model is trained on the ranked dataset, as proxy to the human (or AI) raters; 4. the language model is fine-tuned with the learned preference model using reinforcement learning.
label: none

sentence: By contrast, we would like to highlight the differences in objective, non-interactive offline learning problem setting, and optimization procedure flexibility: First, Objective: The objective of Prompt- OIRL is to evaluate and optimize prompting strategies, rather than enhance LLMs’ alignment to non-differentiable objectives.
label: none

sentence: Importantly, the learned reward model in Prompt-OIRL can work in isolation as a prompt evaluator.
label: none

sentence: Second, Non-Interactive Offline Setting: Prompt-OIRL works in a purely offline setting, rather than assuming access to human or AI raters to actively generate feed- back.
label: none

sentence: Third, the optimization procedure in Prompt-OIRL is highly flexible, which is not necessary to be a language model as in RLHF and RLAIF.
label: none

sentence: For instance, the prompt optimization process can collaborate with a human prompting engineer, who proposes potential prompting strategies and selects the best according to the learned reward model.

sentence: However, running retrieval- augmented language models (LMs) is slow and difficult to scale due to processing large amounts of retrieved text.

sentence: However, this approach is slow (e.g., only handles a few queries for a powerful server GPU) at inference time mainly due to the reader model that needs to compute cross-attention between the input query and a large number of passages.
label: none

sentence: Existing solutions (Lee et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2020) improve the inference computation by decomposing query and passage encoding and precomputing passage representations, but they come with large storage costs (terabytes of storage; §4).
label: none

sentence: In this work, we improve the inference speed of the reader model in a retrieval-augmented LM with a small storage footprint by introducing cacheable and calibrated B inary T oken R epresentations ( BTR ).
label: none

sentence: BTR (Figure 1) precomputes token representations for the retrieved passages in the reader model.
label: none

sentence: The binary representations are 1-bit vectors for the tokens in a passage and are created from the hidden states in the reader encoder layers via calibrated binarization which are effective for downstream tasks such as question answering.
label: none

sentence: BTR reduces the storage footprint and improves the runtime speed since the representations are 1-bit vectors, and the reader uses the cached representations.
label: none

sentence: To avoid degradation of task accuracy caused by binary representations, we introduce two training objectives by adding (i) a passage representation recovery objective that makes the binary representations preserve the passage semantics before the binarization; and (ii) a query-aware passage token distillation objective that compensates the information loss due to precompuation of passage representations independent of the query.
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, we observe significant redundancies in precomputed token representations in retrieved passages since they are relevant to the query and contain similar information.

sentence: We evaluate BTR on five knowledge-rich NLP tasks, including three open-domain question- answering tasks (NaturalQuestions (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), and WebQA (Berant et al., 2013) ), the FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018) fact-checking task, and the MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020) reasoning benchmark.

sentence: The training regulariza- tion objectives help mitigate the task accuracy loss and the offline and runtime token compression techniques further bring down storage footprint and increase inference efficiency. 2 B ACKGROUND AND R ELATED WORK We first describe the architecture of retrieval-augmented language models and then related efficiency techniques designed for them.

sentence: Next, we summarize relevant methods to improve model efficiency, including quantization and binary representations.

sentence: As shown in Figure 1, a retrieval-augmented language model works by first using a retriever to retrieve many passages relevant to the input query and then using a reader component to extract or generate the answers.
label: none

sentence: While the retriever is often fast enough, the reader causes a speed bottleneck in retrieval augmentation because it requires computing cross-attention between the input query and many passages.
label: none

sentence: For example, Figure 1 illustrates a state-of-the-art encoder-decoder reader (Izacard et al., 2022b) architecture called Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) (Izacard & Grave, 2021).
label: none

sentence: FiD first concatenates each passage with the query and processes them in parallel (independently) in the encoder; then the decoder fuses information across all the concatenated passage-query representations and produces answers.
label: none

sentence: In our experiments, we observe that the passage encoding takes over 60% of the reader’s computation on commodity GPUs, and we save such computations by precomputing the passage representations, leading to significant speedup in the inference with reduced storage costs.
label: none

sentence: DensePhrase (Lee et al., 2021) builds contextualized phrase representations for the passage corpus, completely removes the reader component, and uses phrase retrieval to produce answers for the query.
label: none

sentence: Despite its high inference throughput, the accuracy is much lower than similar size BTR models.
label: none

sentence: FiD-light (Hofstätter et al., 2022) and FiDO (de Jong et al., 2022) focus on improving the inference latency for FiD models on customized hardware like TPUs, they compress passage representations into fixed-size vectors to reduce the decoder computation. 2 Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024 But on more popular hardware like GPUs, the passage encoder is the computation bottleneck, and their decoder-oriented optimizations are likely to be less effective in improving inference speed.

sentence: We add a passage representation recovery loss L to the original task recovery loss L task (described below).
label: none

sentence: Decomposing passages encoding from the query in the lower layers of the reader encoder often causes task performance degradation.
label: none

sentence: Previous work (Cao et al., 2020) distilled upper-layer passage representations in the decomposed reader encoder from the original (not decomposed) model to reduce information loss due to decomposition.
label: none

sentence: We empirically find that the direct application of this distillation does not improve the task performance much for a retrieval-augmented LM.
label: none

sentence: This is likely because DeFormer-style distillation applies to single passage scenarios where all passage tokens are important to the task, whereas in our setting the reader retrieves many passages that may contain more redundant passage token information.
label: none

sentence: Distilling all token representations using Cao et al. (2020) from all retrieved passages distracts the reader encoder and makes it fail to pass useful passage token information for the task.
label: none

sentence: To address this issue, we design a query-aware passage token distillation loss to improve the decom- posed passage representation quality.
label: none

sentence: We only distill the passage tokens that are semantically relevant (salient) to the query from the original (non-decomposed) model.
label: none

sentence: This is because query-relevant passage tokens carry more fine-grained query-related information from the original (not decomposed) passage representations.
label: none

label: none

sentence: Next, BTR reader converts the loaded binary token representations into continuous 6 float-point vectors and concatenates them with query representations before layer k + 1 .
label: none

sentence: Then from layer k + 1 to layer n in the reader encoder, BTR applies runtime compression (described below) over the concatenated query-passage representations to reduce the number of tokens and further speed up the encoder inference.
label: none

sentence: Once the encoder finishes computation, the reader flattens and concatenates all the query-passage representations, and then feeds them into the reader decoder.
label: none

sentence: The reader decoder applies similar runtime compression operations to shorten the concatenated text sequence with query and all passage tokens.
label: none

sentence: Runtime compression is possible because the retrieved passages are relevant to the query and contain similar information for different passages.
label: none

sentence: The runtime token compression consists of intra-passage and cross-passage compression steps.
label: none

sentence: At the upper layers ( k + 1 to n ) in the reader encoder, the query representations are concatenated with representations of each passage, and the query-passage representations are processed together.
label: none

sentence: We compress the token representations of each query-passage pair and call this process intra-passage token compression since the encoder still computes each query-passage pair representation in parallel.
label: none

sentence: After the encoder computation, all the query-passage representations are flattened and concatenated.
label: none

sentence: In the reader decoder, we further compress the resulting representations across all passages (and the query) for every g layer 7 and call this cross-passage token compression.
label: none

sentence: We use a similar compression algorithm as in the offline token compression, merging r % tokens based on their semantic similarity.
label: none

sentence: The difference here is that p the representations are continuous vectors in the upper encoder and the decoder, so we change the similarity metric to cosine distance accordingly.

sentence: This generation process usually requires the identification of the disentangled latent representations, such as content and style, that underlie the observed data.

sentence: However, it becomes more challenging when faced with a scarcity of paired data and labeling information.
label: none

sentence: Existing disentangled methods crucially rely on oversimplified assumptions, such as assuming independent content and style variables, to identify the latent variables, even though such assumptions may not hold for complex data distributions.
label: none

sentence: For tasty instance, food reviews tend to involve words like “ ”, whereas movie reviews commonly contain words such as “ thrilling ” for the same positive sentiment.

sentence: This problem is exacerbated when data are sampled from multiple domains since the dependence between content and style may vary significantly over domains.
label: none

sentence: In this work, we tackle the domain-varying dependence between the content and the style variables inherent in the counterfactual generation task.
label: none

sentence: We provide identification guarantees for such latent-variable models by leveraging the relative sparsity of the influences from different latent variables.
label: none

label: none

sentence: Our theoretically grounded framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised style transfer tasks, where neither paired data nor style labels are utilized, across four large-scale datasets.
label: none

sentence: Code is available at https://github.com/hanqi-qi/Matte.git. 1 Introduction Counterfactual generation serves as a crucial component in various machine learning applications, such as controllable text generation and image translation.
label: none

sentence: Consequently, the central challenge in counterfactual generation is to learn the underlying disentangled representations.
label: none

sentence: However, collecting paired data or labels can be labour-intensive and even infeasible in many real-world applications [Chou et al., 2022, Calderon et al., 2022, Xie et al., 2023].
label: none

sentence: This has prompted recent work [Kong et al., 2022, Xie et al., 2023] to delve into unsupervised identification of latent variables by tapping into multiple domains.

sentence: However, this assumption is often violated in practical applications.
label: none

sentence: First, the dependence between content and style variables can be highly pronounced.
label: none

sentence: For example, to express a positive sentiment, words such as “ tasty ” and “ flavor ” are typically used in conjunction with food-related content.
label: none

sentence: In contrast, words like “ thrilling ” are more commonly used with movie-related content [Li et al., 2019, 2022].
label: none

sentence: Moreover, the dependence between content and style often varies across different distributions.
label: none

sentence: For example, a particular cuisine may be highly favored locally but not well received internationally.
label: none

sentence: This varying dependence between content and style variables poses a significant challenge in obtaining the identifiability guarantee.
label: none

sentence: To the best of our knowledge, this issue has not been addressed in previous studies.
label: none

sentence: In this paper, we address the identification problem of the latent-variable model that takes into account the varying dependence between content and style (see Fig 1).
label: none

sentence: To this end, we adopt a natural notion of influence sparsity inherent to a range of unstructured data, including natural languages, for which the influences from the content and the style differ in their scopes.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, the influence of the style variable on the text is typically sparser compared to that of the content variable, as it is often localized to a smaller fraction of the words [Li et al., 2018] and plays a secondary role in word selection.
label: none

sentence: For instance, the tense of a sentence is typically reflected in only its verbs which are affected by the sentence content information.
label: none

sentence: Our contributions can be summarised as: 1) We show identification guarantees for both the content and the style components, even when their interdependence varies.
label: none

sentence: This approach removes the necessity for a large number of domains with specific variance properties [Kong et al., 2022, Xie et al., 2023]. 2) Guided by our theoretical findings, we design a do M ain A dap T ive coun T erfactual g E neration model ( MATTE ).
label: none

sentence: It does not require paired data or style annotations but allows style intervention, even across substantially different domains. 3) We validate our theoretical discoveries by demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on the unsupervised style transfer task, which demands representation disentanglement, an integral aspect of counterfactual generation. 2 Related work Label-free Style Transfer on variation autoencoders (VAEs).
label: none

sentence: To perform style transfer, existing methods that use parallel or non-parallel labelled data often rely on style annotations to refine the attribute-bearing representations, although some argue that disentanglement is not necessary for style edit [Sudhakar et al., 2019, Wang et al., 2019a, Dai et al., 2019].
label: none

sentence: Several studies have tackled this task without style labels.
label: none

sentence: Riley et al. [2020] emphasized the implicit style connection between adjacent sentences and used T5 [Raffel et al., 2020] to extract the style vector for conditional generation.

sentence: CPVAE Xu et al. [2020] split the latent variable into content and style variables and mapped them to a k -dimensional simplex for k -way sentiment modeling.

sentence: Representation learning serves as the cornerstone for generative models, where the goal is to create representations that effectively capture underlying factors in the disentangled data-generation process.

sentence: In the realm of linear generative functions, Independent component analysis (ICA) [Comon, 1994, Bell and Sejnowski, 1995] is a classical approach known for its identifiability.

sentence: However, these approaches require a number of domains/classes that are twice the number of latent components, which can be unfeasible when dealing with high-dimensional representations.

sentence: The third line of work [Lachapelle et al., 2022, Yang et al., 2022, Zheng et al., 2022] makes sparsity assumptions on the nonlinear generating function.

sentence: Although their sparsity assumption alleviates some of the explicit requirements 2 in the previous two types of work, it may not hold for complex data distributions.

sentence: Language models often make mistakes in these types of difficult calculations.
label: none

sentence: This is usually explained by their inability to perform complex rea- soning.
label: none

sentence: Since language models rely on large training sets and great memorization capabil- ity, naturally they are not equipped to run complex calculations.
label: none

sentence: However, one can argue that humans also cannot perform this calculation immediately and require a considerable amount of time to construct the solution.
label: none

sentence: In order to enhance the generalization capability of language models, and as a parallel to human behavior, we propose to use special ’think- ing tokens’ which allow the model to perform much more calculations whenever a complex problem is encountered. 1 Introduction Language models based on neural networks have gained a great deal of interest in recent years [ 15 , 14 ].
label: none

sentence: Their impressive and coherent answers amazed people across many industries.
label: none

sentence: How- ever, it has soon been discovered that these language models have problems with complex tasks [ 5 , 4 ].
label: none

sentence: Complex questions such as ’how much is 56 times 37’ which are computationally requiring, are problematic for the language model to process or even answer correctly.
label: none

sentence: One can argue that humans also cannot perform this calculation right away and require a considerable amount of time to provide a solution.
label: none

sentence: Although these reasoning abilities could be improved by employing a large amount of supervision by providing labeled examples to the model [ 4 ], we aim for a much faster unsu- pervised approach.
label: none

sentence: To enhance the generalization capability of language models, we propose to use special ’thinking tokens’ which allow the model to Figure 1: Illustration of ’thinking tokens’ (marked perform much more calculations whenever a as < T > ) in a sentence which requires a complex complex problem is encountered.
label: none

sentence: This could calculation and the positive impact of this approach result in an improved generalization capabil- on perplexity of the model (lower is better). ity of language models, which could adapt to more complex tasks and even decide themselves what strategy is most beneficial for an encoun- tered problem. 2 Related work Research regarding reasoning can be traced back to 1959 [ 16 ], and now continues to be a big part of theorem proving [ 18 , 6 , 8 ].
label: none

sentence: Presently, large language models are being used to learn reasoning from natural language [ 1 , 11 ].
label: none

sentence: Thinking Tokens for Language Modeling David Herel, Tomas Mikolov A similar problem has also been studied in [ 9 ], where a language model recomputes only a part of the recurrent hidden layer.
label: none

sentence: Another work with a similar motivation explores the possibility of using a neural network that is capable of learning algorithms [ 10 ]. 3 Thinking tokens for language models Our approach is to introduce special ’thinking tokens’ ( < T > ) after each word in a sentence whenever a complex problem is encountered.
label: none

sentence: The core idea is that each ’thinking token’ would buy more time for the model before an answer is expected, which would be used to run additional computations to better answer a complex problem that was presented.
label: none

sentence: This concept has a great potential in recurrent neural networks [ 3 , 7 ] due to their architecture, because it enables the RNN to perform multiple in-memory operations in a single step, meaning that extra calculations can be run in the hidden layer multiple times.
label: none

sentence: As a proof of concept, we have added N ’thinking tokens’ ( < T > ) after each observed word in a dataset.
label: none

sentence: Our vision is that this basic concept can be extended to a self-adjusting model, which will be able to decide itself if and how many ’thinking tokens’ will be used for a specific problem, where N could also vary throughout the sentence.
label: none

sentence: This would allow us to reduce the computational time, which would not increase N times.
label: none

sentence: The visualization of our core idea, which we aim to validate in this paper, is presented in Figure 1 . 4 Results Experiments execution has successfully produced numerous examples where the usage of ’think- ing tokens’ leads to an improvement in the model’s judgment.

sentence: Preliminary results show that sentences that require non-trivial reasoning, have the biggest improvement in perplexity when ’thinking tokens’ are used compared to the standard model.

sentence: FairFlow: An Automated Approach to Model-based Counterfactual Data Augmentation For NLP Ewoenam Kwaku Tokpo and Toon Calders University of Antwerp, Antwerp, Belgium arXiv:2407.16431v1 [cs.CL] 23 Jul 2024 { ewoenamkwaku.tokpo,toon.calders } @uantwerpen.be Abstract.
label: none

sentence: Despite the evolution of language models, they continue to portray harmful societal biases and stereotypes inadvertently learned from training data.
label: none

sentence: These inherent biases often result in detrimental ef- fects in various applications.
label: none

sentence: Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), which seeks to balance demographic attributes in training data, has been a widely adopted approach to mitigate bias in natural language process- ing.
label: none

sentence: However, many existing CDA approaches rely on word substitution techniques using manually compiled word-pair dictionaries.
label: none

sentence: These tech- niques often lead to out-of-context substitutions, resulting in potential quality issues.
label: none

sentence: The advancement of model-based techniques, on the other hand, has been challenged by the need for parallel training data.
label: none

sentence: Works in this area resort to manually generated parallel data that are expen- sive to collect and are consequently limited in scale.
label: none

sentence: This paper proposes FairFlow, an automated approach to generating parallel data for training counterfactual text generator models that limits the need for human in- tervention.
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, we show that FairFlow significantly overcomes the limitations of dictionary-based word-substitution approaches whilst maintaining good performance.
label: none

sentence: Keywords: Natural language processing · Bias mitigation · Counterfac- tual Data Augmentation 1 Introduction Despite their growing popularity and unprecedented performance in various ap- plication domains, language models (LMs) continue to be plagued with issues of harmful societal biases and stereotypes that have been shown to have detrimental social effects [4].
label: none

sentence: The biggest contributing factor is the encapsulation of societal biases in everyday language, as is well-documented [1,19,12].
label: none

sentence: LMs heavily rely on such textual data, now digitalized on various online outlets, as training data, causing them to mirror these biases [25].
label: none

sentence: In Natural Language Processing (NLP), similar to many machine learning do- mains, bias mitigation generally occurs at three intervention avenues: the train- ing data, the learning procedure, or the model output [15].
label: none

sentence: Since model bias traces its roots to the training data, mitigating bias at the training data level 2 E.
label: none

sentence: Tokpo et al. has proven very effective [10,6].
label: none

sentence: One such approach, Counterfactual Data Aug- mentation (CDA) [5], seeks to remove spurious correlations between attributes in the training data by evening out the distribution of words that characterize demographic attributes in the context of neutral words that should ideally not be demographically aligned.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, explicit attribute-defining words are re- placed with their counterfactual equivalents from complementary demographic groups for every text instance.
label: none

sentence: To illustrate this with an example, an instance of “ She is a nurse ” will be augmented with “ He is a nurse ” in the case of mitigating gender bias.
label: none

sentence: This follows the intuition that in an ideal dataset, the association between gender attributes and target attributes like professions will be even for different gender groups.
label: none

sentence: Key works, such as [27,16,28], introducing CDA as a bias mitigation tech- nique adopt a word substitution approach based on dictionaries.
label: none

sentence: These word substitution methods are prone to grammatical incoherence because of out-of- context substitutions and omitted word pairs.
label: none

sentence: Because dictionary compilations are often incomplete [8], a direct word-substitution approach will not generalize to omitted words.
label: none

sentence: Take for instance ( Bachelor and Masters degree v.
label: none

sentence: Spin- ster and Mistresses degree ) and ( she taught herself v. he taught herself ) which were common issues we observed with some methods.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, the dictionaries are manually compiled, which not only incurs potential costs but manually compiling counterfactual word pairs for certain demographics may be intrinsically challenging.
label: none

sentence: Although generative language models like GPT-related models [21] have surged in popularity, their adoption for CDA has been limited due to the rel- ative unavailability of parallel data needed for training.
label: none

sentence: As such, model-based solutions resort to manually compiling parallel training data, a process that is both costly and constrained.
label: none

sentence: This challenge is exacerbated by the fact that train- ing models on limited parallel data can impair performance [29].
label: none

sentence: Although large conversational models like ChatGPT generate good counterfactuals in a zero- shot setting, they are not efficient in low-resource environments.
label: none

sentence: In this work, we focus on low-resource/resource-efficient techniques that can be deployed in low-resource environments.
label: none

sentence: The primary contribution of this paper is to explore an automated approach to generate parallel training data for a given demographic axis that requires minimal human intervention.
label: none

sentence: Our approach takes from a user a prompt – in the form of a single word-pair – that describes a demographic axis.
label: none

sentence: This pair is subsequently used to model a demographic subspace from which other words that define the demographic attribute can be sampled from a given corpus of text.
label: none

sentence: Using an invertible flow-based model [9], counterfactual words are generated for sampled words.
label: none

sentence: Thereafter, an error correction approach is used in tandem with direct word substitution to generate parallel data to fine-tune a generative language model to generate counterfactual texts.
label: none

sentence: We call our approach and the resultant counterfactual text generation model FairFlow .
label: none

sentence: This entire process is simply depicted in a four-step process in Fig. 1.
label: none

sentence: As opposed to existing works, which will be discussed in Section 2, FairFlow does not rely on human-generated FairFlow 3 parallel data for training and eliminates the need for manually compiled word- pair dictionaries.
label: none

label: none

sentence: An end-to-end description of Fairflow, described in four steps: 1) train a classi- fier to identify attribute words from a corpus; 2) generate counterfactual equivalents for attribute words using an invertible generative flow model; 3) use a word substitution scheme and our proposed error-correction scheme to make the parallel text more fluent and realistic; 4) fine-tune a generative model with the generated parallel data.
label: none

sentence: In summary, this paper explores and proposes techniques to develop a robust model-based counterfactual generator in the absence of parallel training data.
label: none

sentence: An automated approach to compiling dictionaries of word pairs that only requires a user to input a word-pair prompt that describes a demographic axis. 2.

sentence: Tokpo et al. 1 We make our implementation code and materials for FairFlow available . 2 Background and Related Literature Early works on CDA used simple rule-based word-substitution approaches for counterfactual data augmentation.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, they created dictionaries of at- tribute word pairs and used matching rules to swap words [6].
label: none

sentence: Later works be- gan to incorporate grammatical information like part-of-speech tags to swap attribute words [27].
label: none

sentence: In the absence of interventions for named entities, Lu et al. [16] do not augment sentences or text instances containing proper nouns, and named entities as generating counterfactuals without proper name interventions could result in semantically incorrect sentences.
label: none

sentence: Zhao et al. [27] circumvented this by anonymizing named entities by replacing them with special tokens.
label: none

sentence: Lamenting on the aforementioned lack of parallel corpus for training neural models, Zmi- grod et al. [28] used a series of unsupervised techniques such as dependency trees, lemmata, part-of-speech tags, and morpho-syntactic tags for counterfactual gen- eration.
label: none

sentence: Hall-Maudsley et al. [17] improve on Zmigrod et al. by incorporating a names intervention method to resolve the challenges of generating counterfactu- als for named entities.
label: none

sentence: They achieve this using a bipartite graph to match first names.
label: none

sentence: Because the aforementioned techniques rely on dictionary word replacement techniques and ignore the context of the text, they are prone to generating ungrammatical texts.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, the inability of these techniques to resolve out-of-dictionary words not only preserves certain attribute correlations but also introduces errors.
label: none

sentence: Wu et al. [26] propose Polyjuice, a generative counterfactual model for diverse use cases like counterfactual expla- nations.
label: none

sentence: They generate parallel data by pairing naturally occurring sentences in a corpus based on edit distances.
label: none

sentence: Although effective for explanations, such an approach is not applicable for bias mitigation as attribute words, in the case of the latter, have to be specifically defined and replaced.
label: none

sentence: Specifically for bias mitigation, Qian et al. [20] introduce the perturber , which is a Bart[14] model fine-tuned on a human-generated parallel text.
label: none

sentence: As earlier stated, such manually compiled datasets are expensive and are only available on small scales, which can degrade performance [29].
label: none

sentence: Addition- ally, similar manual efforts must be solicited for every language domain for which counterfactuals have to be generated.

sentence: Finite-State Machine A finite-state machine starts out in a given internal state, reads some symbol from some input, and based on that symbol, might change its internal state.

sentence: There are a finite number of states and a finite number of symbols.

sentence: The operation of such a machine is as follows: the machine starts out in a given internal state.
label: none

sentence: In a first step, it reads a symbol from the tape at the current position of its head.
label: none

sentence: Depending on a set of rules described in the state-transition table, the machine either switches its internal state to a new state or remains in the same state.
label: none

sentence: Finally, the head is moved to the next position, and the process starts all over again.

sentence: Discussion The key contributions of this work include the realization that the Decoder machine from [1] can function as a finite-state machine, formalization of a Turing Machine capable of self-replication, and demonstration of universality via the UTM(5,5) model.

sentence: This marks a step forward in the field of molecular computing and mechanical self-replication, and provides new insights into how such systems can be designed.

sentence: The use of the Decoder machine as a finite-state machine capable of performing basic computational tasks may come as a surprise, but it lies in the fact that the tRNA are basically lookup tables, wherein the true computational power lies, and clearly shows that computational power is at the heart of self-replicating machines, that is biological cells.
label: none

sentence: The finite-state machine (FSM) essentially operates in the same way as the Decoder, which mirrors the function of the ribosome in biological systems, with the primary difference being the type of tRNA involved.
label: none

sentence: Thus, if a FSM were advantageous to a living cell, evolution could have easily produced one.
label: none

sentence: This raises an interesting question: can a FSM serve a useful function within a cell?
label: none

sentence: Finite-state machines are very useful in various computational tasks such as counting, basic forms of computation, parsing, pattern recognition, controlling, verification, and modeling.
label: none

sentence: For instance, a simple FSM could allow a cell to generate periodic signals or track how frequently a certain event occurred.
label: none

sentence: In the context of cellular communication, cells or organelles within a cell could potentially exchange short RNA sequences as a means of communicating information, which FSMs could then read and interpret.
label: none

sentence: Such FSMs could also be applied to biological processes such as building complex structures.
label: none

sentence: For example, in organisms that construct shells, FSMs might be used to create periodic or patterned designs.
label: none

sentence: The concept of mechanical computation could prove valuable at the cellular level, similar to how cells respond to sensor inputs or store and process information.
label: none

sentence: This flexibility represents the essence of computing, that is, the ability to generate entirely new outcomes based on external conditions.
label: none

sentence: Unlike simple biological replication or mutation, computational systems allow responses to sensory inputs and dynamic problem-solving.
label: none

sentence: However, when considering more complex machines such as Turing machines (TM), we need to assess their practicality in biological contexts.
label: none

sentence: The TM proposed in this work is one orders of magnitude more efficient than that described in [3].

sentence: Ontology Alignment (OA) is fundamental for achieving se- mantic interoperability across diverse knowledge systems.
label: none

sentence: We present OntoAligner, a comprehensive, modular, and robust Python toolkit for ontology alignment, designed to address current limitations with exist- ing tools faced by practitioners.
label: none

sentence: Existing tools are limited in scalability, modularity, and ease of integration with recent AI advances.
label: none

sentence: OntoAligner provides a flexible architecture integrating existing lightweight OA tech- niques such as fuzzy matching but goes beyond by supporting con- temporary methods with retrieval-augmented generation and large lan- guage models for OA.
label: none

sentence: The framework prioritizes extensibility, enabling researchers to integrate custom alignment algorithms and datasets.
label: none

sentence: This paper details the design principles, architecture, and implementation of the OntoAligner, demonstrating its utility through benchmarks on stan- dard OA tasks.
label: none

sentence: Our evaluation highlights OntoAligner’s ability to handle large-scale ontologies efficiently with few lines of code while delivering high alignment quality.
label: none

sentence: By making OntoAligner open-source, we aim to provide a resource that fosters innovation and collaboration within the OA community, empowering researchers and practitioners with a toolkit for reproducible OA research and real-world applications.
label: none

sentence: However, evolving sys- tems within the semantic web generally adopt different ontologies [10].

sentence: Hence, OA, the process of identifying correspondences between entities in different on- tologies, spans various domains, including semantic web services, biomedical re- search, and KG integration.
label: none

sentence: Despite significant advancements in OA research (cf. [32,27]), practitioners still face challenges related to scalability, modularity, ro- bustness, and reproducibility when developing or deploying alignment systems.
label: none

sentence: Many existing tools struggle with scalability when processing large ontologies, lack modularity to accommodate diverse use cases, and fall short in integrating contemporary AI methodologies.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, limited support for customiza- tion, coupled with sparse documentation, creates barriers to adoption in both academic and industrial contexts.
label: none

sentence: These limitations underscore the urgent need for a robust, flexible, and user-friendly OA framework that can cater to the evolving demands of modern applications.
label: none

sentence: Building on previous investigations, we observed a prevailing trend in OA is the use of large language models (LLMs), as highlighted by several studies [20,17,33,40,4,45,41,42].

sentence: However, addressing the challenges within OA frame- works requires more than simply leveraging LLMs.

sentence: Motivated by our prior re- search on the empirical evaluation of LLMs for OA [5] and the growing interest in LLM-driven approaches (as a starting point), we introduce OntoAligner, a comprehensive Python-based toolkit designed to advance the state of OA tools.
label: none

sentence: OntoAligner adopts a modular architecture that seamlessly integrates traditional heuristic methods, retrieval-based models, and cutting-edge LLMs such as (but not limited to) Mistral [21], LLaMA [44], Falcon [3], and Qwen [6].
label: none

sentence: The toolkit provides a flexible framework for OA, allowing users to configure and customize alignment algorithms, incorporate new datasets, and fine-tune pipelines with minimal effort.
label: none

sentence: This modularity ensures that OntoAligner can adapt to a wide range of use cases, from lightweight heuristic alignments to advanced scenarios leveraging retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [13] and in-context learning (ICL) [8].
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, OntoAligner emphasizes scalability, efficiently handling large and complex ontologies by optimizing memory usage and computational performance.
label: none

sentence: OntoAligner introduces several key features that distinguish it from exist- ing tools.
label: none

sentence: It combines traditional methods like fuzzy matching with advanced techniques such as RAG and ICL to ensure high alignment quality.
label: none

sentence: Its intuitive design supports both step-by-step workflows and integrated pipelines, enabling users to tailor alignment processes to their needs.
label: none

sentence: The toolkit also provides com- prehensive evaluation metrics, such as precision, recall, and F1-score, alongside robust post-processing methods to ensure the consistency of alignment outputs.
label: none

sentence: OntoAligner facilitates extensibility, allowing researchers to integrate custom alignment algorithms, post-processing steps, and evaluation modules.
label: none

sentence: Moreover, the toolkit’s extensive documentation, tutorials, and examples enhance its ac- cessibility for users with varying levels of expertise.

sentence: We detail the implementation of the core components of OntoAligner and their respective functionalities. 1) Parser Module.
label: none

sentence: This module consists of two important components, Align- ment and Ontology parsers.
label: none

sentence: The ontology parsing module supports the ingestion of ontologies in standardized formats such as OWL and RDF, either from local files or remote URLs (F1, F2).
label: none

sentence: The parsing process extracts essential meta- data, including class and property names, IRIs, hierarchical structures, syn- onyms, and annotations, enabling compatibility with diverse ontology structures.
label: none

sentence: However, advanced metadata (e.g., highly expressive OWL axioms) may require further processing or adaptations in future versions to support alignment al- gorithms with different metadata needs.
label: none

sentence: This functionality is encapsulated in the class, which is the foundation for downstream alignment OntologyParser tasks.
label: none

sentence: Moreover, the alignment parser encapsulated in the AlignmentsParser class loads ground truth alignments for OA tasks, which will later be used to evaluate alignment efficiency. 2) Encoder Module.
label: none

sentence: After parsing the alignment ontologies, the framework employs multiple encoders to effectively represent ontological concepts in suitable data structures (e.g., natural language text or paired concepts for later similar- ity estimation) for subsequent processing.
label: none

sentence: Drawing insights from the previous study on ontology representations in [5], this module utilizes Concept C (ba- sic concept representation), Concept-Children CC (lower-level taxonomy), and 8 Babaei Giglou.
label: none

sentence: H et al. Concept-Parent CP (upper-level taxonomy) as foundational metadata.
label: none

sentence: These representations serve as the basis for the following encoders, which are designed as modular components and include: – Lightweight Encoder.
label: none

sentence: This utilizes forming inputs as a raw text, which is a simple lightweight approach for heuristic techniques such as Fuzzy Matching and Retrieval Matching for computationally inexpensive alignments.
label: none

sentence: For C , CC , and CP , it just combines concepts with respective pairs in a natural language text. – LLM Encoder.
label: none

sentence: It uses the desired representation to clean the text and obtain parents and children in desirable formatting (each concept and its combined parents stored in a dictionary) for integrating into prompt placeholders for inferences with LLMs. – RAG Encoder.
label: none

sentence: Aims to provide structured inputs for both retriever and LLMs in leveraging RAG [25] with Few-Shot and ICL– specifically we incor- porated the in-context vectors (ICV) approach introduced by Liu et al. [26] as an aligner which requires encoder – for advanced alignment scenarios.
label: none

sentence: This modular design (F3) allows users to choose and configure the most suitable encoder for their specific use case (F4). 3) Aligner Module.
label: none

sentence: The core alignment process is performed by the Aligners module for the alignment algorithm, which includes several predefined categories: – Lightweight Aligners.
label: none

sentence: Fast and heuristic-based algorithms for mappings be- tween entities.
label: none

sentence: Lightweight aligners include fuzzy matchings [36] such as simple token sets and weighted fuzzy matching models that take matching thresholds to perform alignments. – Retrieval Aligners .
label: none

sentence: A machine learning model is designed to retrieve matches based on semantic similarity or keyword matching.
label: none

sentence: They mostly operate on semantic similarity techniques using vector representations.
label: none

sentence: Retrieval align- ers within OntoAligner consist of sentence-transformer [34]-based, TFIDF, and SVM [24] models.
label: none

sentence: The sentence-transformer module is compatible with a wide range of transformer models from Hugging Face, including both official models and community-contributed models. – LLM Aligners .
label: none

sentence: An LLM-based approach that leverages LLMs from the Hug- ging Face repository for alignment.
label: none

sentence: These aligners operate using predefined prompts to query LLMs (the prompts have been discussed within [5]), deter- mining whether a match exists between pairs of concepts.
label: none

sentence: This set of aligners operates with quadratic time complexity but remains practical for smaller ontology alignment tasks involving fewer than ≈ 200 concepts in the source and target ontologies. – RAG Aligners .
label: none

sentence: A hybrid alignment method that integrates retrieval and generative capabilities of LLMs to produce high-quality alignments.
label: none

sentence: These aligners retrieve relevant knowledge before generating alignment decisions, enhancing accuracy and contextual understanding.
label: none

sentence: On the LLM side, instead of relying on full-text generation, OntoAligner utilizes logit-based probabil- ity calculations to determine alignments.
label: none

sentence: This reduces the token sampling OntoAligner 9 overhead associated with text generation, which allows them to operate on the single forward pass.
label: none

sentence: The framework allows users to configure these algorithms, ensuring flexibility and adaptability to various OA scenarios (F4).
label: none

sentence: Moreover, the Post-Processing steps are implemented to refine the initial mappings generated by the align- ers.
label: none

sentence: These include LLM-based mapping (mapping generated natural language to the pre-defined classes) and rule-based and heuristic filtering/processing ad- justments to ensure the consistency and quality of alignments (F7, N6).
label: none

sentence: The modular nature of the post-processing pipeline enables easy integration of addi- tional refinement techniques.
label: none

sentence: The post-processing module is being implemented as different components to support users’ desirable post-processing algorithms for different models.
label: none

sentence: The Mapper is a post-processing technique that is useful for assigning appropriate labels to generated LLM texts, especially in LLM Aligner . 4) Evaluation and Exporter Modules.
label: none

sentence: To assess the quality of generated alignments, the framework includes an Evaluator module that computes stan- dard metrics such as precision, recall, and F-measure (F9).
label: none

sentence: Users can also com- pare mappings produced by different algorithms or configurations (F10).
label: none

sentence: The final mappings can be exported in widely used formats, including XML and JSON, via the Exporter module (F8).
label: none

sentence: The OntoAligner framework is designed for extensibility, allowing developers to add custom alignment algorithms or modify existing ones through a well- documented API (F11, F12).
label: none

sentence: The code base adheres to modular object-oriented design principles, promoting ease of maintenance and scalability (N8) while allowing base foundational modules for extensions based on newer alignment frameworks.
label: none

sentence: To handle large ontologies efficiently, OntoAligner optimizes mem- ory usage and computational performance, enabling the alignment of ontologies containing thousands of classes and properties within a reasonable time frame (N1, N2).
label: none

sentence: Additionally, the framework includes good documentation, user guides, and tutorials to ensure accessibility for users of varying expertise levels (N3, N4).
